description: We build software designed to keep astronauts safe and healthy. By gathering biometric data from wearables like smartwatches and oxygen sensors, our AI analyzes health and sleep trends in real time. We deliver actionable insights to astronauts through a clear, intuitive dashboard and direct AI voice interaction.
summary:
ExoLab — We watch the vitals so you can focus on the stars.

ExoLab is an ML-and-DL-backed astronaut health monitoring system designed to help crews stay in good health during long-duration space missions, where immediate medical assistance from Earth may be impossible.

Our vision combines data from wearable sensors, medical measurements, and spacecraft environmental monitors to monitor six critical health sectors: cardiovascular health, behavioral health and stress, bone and muscle health, immunity, radiation safety, and sleep.

As our first proof of concept, we developed a lightweight neural network trained on real physiological data (from WESAD) to recognize stress-related patterns. Tested on previously unseen participants, it achieved 81.4% accuracy and 92% stress precision and was successfully exported to TensorFlow Lite for mobile integration via our flutter-based app.

Our ultimate goal is to provide a user friendly application that monitors the astronaut's health metrics, explains their health status, issues, and suggestive actions back to them in a human and concise way, follows up with them on the suggestive actions, and documents the improvement or deterioration of their health due to these actions, enabling consent-based communication with medical professionals.

ExoLab aims to make space healthcare more accessible, proactive, and autonomous.
details:
The Problem

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to significant physiological and psychological risks, including cardiovascular deterioration, bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, immune system changes, sleep disruption, and behavioral stress.

As missions travel farther from Earth, communication delays and limited access to medical professionals make astronauts increasingly responsible for monitoring and managing their own health.

ExoLab aims to bridge this gap by bringing intelligent, understandable health monitoring directly onboard the spacecraft.

Our Solution

ExoLab is an AI-powered astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to transform complex physiological measurements into clear, personalized insights and actionable recommendations.

Our proposed system monitors six health sectors:

  1. Cardiovascular health
  2. Behavioral health and stress
  3. Bone and muscle health
  4. Immune system health
  5. Radiation safety
  6. Sleep and fatigue

The system is designed to gather information from wearable sensors, medical examinations, spacecraft environmental measurements, and astronaut inputs.

Rather than requiring astronauts to interpret medical data themselves, ExoLab aims at explaining the significance of detected patterns in simple, accessible language.

How ExoLab Works

Our proposed architecture follows four main stages:

1. Data Acquisition: Collect physiological measurements, medical information, and environmental data.

2. Intelligent Analysis: Process the measurements and route relevant features into six specialized machine-learning models, each responsible for a particular health sector.

3. AI-Powered Interpretation: Combine the models' findings through a locally running large language model (LLM), designed to explain health trends, possible concerns, and appropriate follow-up actions.

4. Astronaut Interaction: Present results through an intuitive Flutter application featuring health dashboards, visualizations, alerts, and an AI assistant.

ExoLab is designed to operate locally, reducing dependence on communication with Earth. The proposed system also supports sharing selected health information with medical professionals, subject to the astronaut's permission.

Our Working Proof of Concept

To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach, we developed a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) for detecting physiological patterns associated with experimentally induced stress.

We trained our model using a preprocessed version of the publicly available WESAD dataset, containing 1,795 labeled observation windows collected from 15 participants.

We selected ten physiological features derived from blood-volume pulse, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and accelerometer measurements.

Our neural network contains two hidden layers with 16 and 8 neurons, respectively, and a single sigmoid output for binary baseline/stress classification.

To evaluate generalization, we separated the participants into nine for training, three for validation, and three for testing.

On the held-out test participants, our model achieved:

  • 81.4% classification accuracy
  • 92% stress precision
  • 54% stress recall

These results demonstrate the feasibility of our lightweight approach while identifying an important limitation: some stress observations remain undetected.

The trained network contains only 321 parameters and was successfully exported to TensorFlow Lite (.tflite) for integration into our Flutter application.

This model represents a research proof of concept, not a clinically validated stress detector.

Technologies Used

Our machine-learning pipeline was developed in Python using Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, and TensorFlow/Keras.

TensorFlow Lite was used to export the trained neural network into a format suitable for mobile inference.

Our application architecture uses Flutter and Dart for the user interface, with FastAPI planned for backend services and Qwen3-4B proposed as a locally running language model for interpreting health data.

The complete six-model architecture, LLM integration, and live sensor-to-prediction workflow remain under development.

Innovation and Creativity

ExoLab's innovation lies in its proposed combination of specialized physiological analysis and accessible, locally generated explanations.

Rather than relying on a single generalized model, our architecture separates health monitoring into six specialized domains whose outputs can be combined into a unified understanding of astronaut health.

This modular approach is intended to make the system easier to extend, validate, and improve independently.

The proposed integration of lightweight machine-learning models, an offline-capable language model, intuitive visualizations, and consent-based medical-data sharing aims to create a comprehensive astronaut health companion.

Intended Impact and Future Development

ExoLab aims to improve astronauts' health awareness and independence, supporting earlier recognition of concerning trends and reducing the burden of interpreting complex medical measurements.

Our next steps include improving stress-detection recall, implementing real-time feature extraction, completing Flutter integration, developing the remaining five health-domain models, and evaluating the complete system using broader and more representative datasets.

We recognize that terrestrial experimental data cannot establish reliability in spaceflight conditions. Future development will require rigorous validation, assessment of false alarms and missed detections, and collaboration with qualified medical professionals.

Our ultimate vision is to give astronauts a dependable health companion that transforms data into understanding, allowing them to focus on exploration while remaining informed about their health.
